question.worked_solution:
Recall that ${f}^{′}(0)$ is just the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $y=f(x)$ at the point where $x=0.$

Notice that our tangent line passes through the points $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(4,0)$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(0,2).$ Therefore, we can compute its slope as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} & =\frac{2-0}{0-4} \\  & =\frac{2}{-4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(0)=-\frac{1}{2}.$

A function $f(x)$ is infinitely differentiable for all real values of its argument $x.$ The graph of $y=f(x)$ and the tangent line to it at the point where $x=0$ are shown above. A few selected derivatives of $f(x)$ at $x=0$ are also given in the table below.

| $n$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{(n)}(0)$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $-1$ | $3$ |

In addition, the function $g$ is defined as 

$$
g(x)={\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Furthermore, it is known that the coefficients of the terms of the Maclaurin series for $g(x)$ form a convergent alternating series $S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
